items.text:
A roofer told me he loses about two jobs a week to voicemail.

Not to a competitor's better price. To voicemail.

He is on a roof. The phone rings. He cannot answer it. The caller does not leave a message, because almost nobody does. They ring the next roofer on the list.

The job was never lost on price or on quality. It was lost because nobody picked up.

I build voice agents that answer those calls, take the name, number, job and address, and text them to the owner within a minute. The owner rings back when they are off the roof, and the caller is still theirs.

If you run a trade and the phone goes unanswered while you work, that is the whole problem worth fixing.

A lot of tradespeople tell me the same thing about AI answering: "My customers won't want to talk to a robot."

Fair worry. But the comparison I'd ask you to make isn't AI versus you. It's AI versus voicemail.

When you're on the tools, the call that goes unanswered isn't answered by you. It goes to a beep, and plenty of callers hang up and ring the next number.

So what would you rather the caller got? A beep, or something that asks what the job is, takes their number and tells them you'll ring back?

If a caller asks whether it's an AI, it says yes. It doesn't quote prices or promise dates. Those stay with you.

Where do you land on that?

I spent a day working out what every AI answering service actually costs, including my own, and wrote it up properly.

One thing that surprised me: the cheap ones advertise minutes, not calls. $29 a month reads well until you realise a proper enquiry runs two to four minutes. That is roughly fifteen calls, and then you are paying by the minute.

The other thing is that the price gap between the cheap ones and the expensive ones is not better technology. It is who does the setting up. Pay less and you write the script and test it yourself. Pay more and somebody else does that part.

So I compared five of them on real prices taken from their own websites, not from a comparison site that earns a commission. That includes two that are cheaper than mine, and who they suit better.

If you have ever wondered whether answering your missed calls is worth paying for, do the sum before you shop. For plenty of businesses the honest answer is no.

items.text:
A short list of things my answering assistant is not allowed to do.

It does not quote a price. Not even a rough one, unless you have given it a range you are happy to stand behind.

It does not promise a date. It has no idea what your week looks like.

It does not argue with anyone or try to sell.

It does not keep ringing someone who has said no.

All it does is pick up, find out what the job is, and get the details to you fast enough that you can still win the work.

Most of building this has been taking things away, not adding them.

What my phone assistant is NOT allowed to do:

Quote a price.
Promise a date.
Try to sell anyone anything.
Pretend to be a person if asked.

What it does: picks up when you can't, finds out what the job is, gets the name, number and address, and texts it to you in about a minute.

The quoting stays with you. That was always the point.

The phone does not stop ringing in winter. It just rings at worse times.

Boilers pack in on the coldest night of the year. Pipes go at six in the morning. A roof starts letting water in during a storm on a Sunday.

Those calls are worth more than the ones at eleven on a Tuesday, because the person ringing is not shopping around. They want someone now.

They are also the calls you are least likely to answer, because you are asleep, or eating, or already out on something else.

This is the gap I built Pulsemint for. Not the easy hours. The expensive ones.

Winter calls are the ones worth having.

New call, 7:42pm. Dave, 07xxx xxxxxx. Shower not draining upstairs, says it has been getting slower for a week. NR33. Asked how soon someone could look. Told him you would ring back tonight or first thing.

That is it. No app to learn, no dashboard to log into, no training.

You read it in ten seconds at the end of a job and decide whether it is worth ringing back tonight.

The best software for someone who works with their hands is usually the software they do not have to think about.

items.text:
Something I changed this month after sitting and listening to call recordings.

The assistant used to ask for the caller's name first. Sensible on paper. In practice it made the call feel like a form being filled in, and a few people got impatient within seconds.

Now it asks what the problem is first, and picks up the name along the way.

Shorter calls, more detail, less of that stiff feeling.

I do not think you can build this sort of thing from a spec. You build a version, you listen to real people talking to it, and you fix what made them hesitate.

Something worth sorting before the end of the month.

Most small firms wind down over Christmas. The phone does not. Boilers still fail, pipes still go, and people still ring round on the 27th looking for anyone who will answer.

The usual plan is a voicemail greeting saying you are back on the 5th. Which politely tells a paying customer to go and find somebody else.

You do not have to work through it. You just have to know who rang, so you can decide what is worth driving out for and what can wait until January.

That is a much nicer problem to have than coming back to an empty diary.
